claims.text: The studied HEA nanoparticles contain 5–8 nearly equimolar elements.
A typical particle-size range for these HEA nanoparticles is 10–50 nm.
Premelting and melting are governed primarily by heterogeneous surface energies.
Local lattice distortions create heterogeneous surface energies in HEA nanoparticles.
Selective elemental segregation at the nanoparticle surface creates heterogeneous surface energies.
High configurational entropy creates nonuniform local bonding environments.
High mixing entropy produces frozen chemical disorder involving local differences in atomic size and bonding.
Chemical disorder promotes preferential surface migration or segregation of elements having lower cohesive energies or melting enthalpies.
Surface enrichment of lower-cohesive-energy elements reduces local cohesion and triggers earlier surface premelting.
Reducing the number of constituent elements reduces configurational entropy.
Binary or ternary nanoparticles have more uniform surfaces than full HEA nanoparticles.
Binary or ternary nanoparticles have higher effective premelting and melting temperatures than full HEA nanoparticles.
Under identical heating conditions, full HEA nanoparticles will show lower surface-premelting onset and overall melting temperatures than reduced-component nanoparticles.
Earlier premelting in full HEA nanoparticles will coincide with a directly observable premelted surface layer and surface enrichment of lower-melting-point elements.
The relevant premelting-to-melting temperature range is approximately 200–500 °C for these nanoparticles.
The proposed effect should hold over an approximately 5–100 nm particle-size range when configurational entropy produces significant lattice distortion.
Bulk materials and clusters smaller than 5 nm may be governed by additional size-dependent or quantum effects.
Interactions with the support may modify nanoparticle premelting behavior.

Failure to observe both a statistically significant lowering of premelting or melting onset and measurable selective surface segregation in full HEA nanoparticles would falsify the proposed mechanism.
